content: Information was collected for each available stratum. The analysis involved pooling data on the median number of days between key steps in the hepatitis C virus (HCV) care cascade. These steps included the time from HCV antibody testing to RNA testing, RNA sample collection to testing, RNA testing to results being made available to the patient, RNA testing to treatment initiation, and anti-HCV testing to treatment initiation. The pooled data were presented by model-of-care categories, using a weighted median of medians approach. This method also generated 95% confidence intervals, enabling comparisons across categories. The weights were determined by the number of patients included at the beginning of each step in each study. A sensitivity analysis was conducted, including only studies with within-study comparisons between arms. The total time from HCV antibody testing to treatment initiation, as well as the percentage of time spent in each care cascade step, was calculated for study arms with available data. Studies where antibody testing and treatment initiation occurred during the same visit were excluded. A weighted average percentage of the total time spent between antibody testing and RNA testing, and between RNA testing and treatment initiation, was calculated, weighted by the number of individuals who started treatment in each arm. Data on cascade outcome proportions were pooled for study arms using point-of-care (PoC) assays and for those using lab-based assays. This was done overall and by model-of-care categorization using random-effects meta-analysis. Confidence intervals were calculated using the exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) method, and the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation was applied to stabilize variances. Pooled proportions were presented for each care cascade step to illustrate attrition at each step and to allow comparisons across studies without comparator arms. Tests for heterogeneity in pooled proportions were performed across model-of-care categories, comparing models 1 and 2 with model 4, models 1 and 2 with model 3, and model 3 with model 4. Heterogeneity tests were also conducted within each model-of-care category (1, 2, 3, and 4). These analyses were performed for all population subgroups combined and for specific subgroups, including people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, general or mixed populations, prisoners, and people living with HIV. The median number of visits required to initiate treatment was reported for each model-of-care categorization for the overall group. To examine the similarities and differences between pooled proportions and individual study results, within-study comparisons of PoC and lab-based arms were conducted where available. Percentages across each pair of arms in the care cascade were compared, and heterogeneity tests were performed for each individual study. For studies with within-study comparisons of PoC and lab-based arms, the relative risks of RNA testing uptake and treatment uptake were calculated and pooled using random-effects meta-analysis. Testing for small-study effects (publication bias) for each cascade outcome proportion was conducted using a regression-based Egger test. The I² statistic was used to measure heterogeneity between study arms within model categorizations. The risk of bias for each study was assessed by two authors using a previously published and modified risk-of-bias tool for observational studies reporting binary outcomes. This tool was based on methods by Hoy et al. and the ROBINS-I tool. Disagreements between the two assessors were resolved by a third author. The strength of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework, considering domains such as risk of bias, consistency of results, directness of evidence, precision of effect estimates, and reporting bias. Based on these assessments, the strength of evidence for each intervention was graded as high, moderate, low, or very low. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) began with a high strength of evidence rating and were downgraded based on the severity of shortcomings in each domain. A high grade indicated high confidence in the evidence reflecting the true effect, while a very low grade indicated insufficient or highly limited evidence. The study identification process included screening 4,492 studies or abstracts from various sources, including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and conference abstracts. Of these, 45 studies were included in the analysis. These studies were geographically distributed and included various population subgroups, such as people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, prisoners, general or mixed populations, and people living with HIV. Most studies were observational, with no RCTs identified. Among the included studies, 36% had a high risk of bias, 40% had a moderate risk, and 24% had a low risk. The studies contributed 64 within-study arms for analysis, including PoC RNA assays and lab-based assay comparator arms. The characteristics of the 64 arms were summarized, with 51 using PoC RNA assays and 13 using lab-based high-throughput RNA assays. PoC RNA assays were predominantly GeneXpert, except for one study in South Africa using GeneDrive. The arms were categorized by model-of-care, including on-site PoC assays, mobile unit PoC assays, off-site lab-based PoC assays, and high-throughput lab-based assays. The median number of days between key steps in the HCV care cascade was analyzed, with significant differences observed between PoC and lab-based assays. PoC assays generally had shorter turnaround times, particularly for RNA testing to treatment initiation. The longest turnaround times were associated with lab-based testing arms. Most differences in time from HCV antibody testing to treatment initiation were attributed to variations in RNA testing to treatment initiation times.
